candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; use precautions to prevent injury or complications associated with procedures; educate clients about treatments and postoperative precautions.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Postoperative precautions and prevention of prosthetic dislocation
candidate.educational_objective: Follow surgeon- and approach-specific hip precautions when they are prescribed after total hip arthroplasty, while recognizing that routine strict posterior precautions are not a universal requirement for every client.

options.A: I will follow the prescribed restrictions, including avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction across the midline, and internal rotation for the period my surgical team specifies.
options.B: All clients with hip replacement require these exact restrictions for the same duration regardless of surgical approach, implant stability, or surgeon protocol.
options.C: Because I feel little pain, I can ignore the prescribed precautions and cross my legs or deeply flex the hip whenever it is comfortable.
options.D: The precautions are intended to prevent blood clots rather than reduce positions that may increase dislocation risk after this posterior approach.

candidate.rationale: A is correct because the stem explicitly states that this client's surgeon prescribed posterior hip precautions. Contemporary randomized evidence shows that routine strict precautions after posterior-approach total hip arthroplasty are not necessarily required for every patient, so the nurse should not teach them as a universal rule. When posterior precautions are prescribed, common restrictions used in trials include avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction across the midline, and internal rotation for the surgeon-specified period. B is incorrect because current evidence does not support presenting the same restrictions and duration as mandatory for every total-hip-replacement client. C is unsafe because the client should follow the individualized postoperative plan rather than use pain absence as permission to disregard prescribed restrictions. D is incorrect because these movement restrictions are intended to reduce provocative hip positions related to dislocation risk, not to serve as venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis. The final item preserves the clinically recognizable posterior-precaution movements while explicitly avoiding an outdated universal-precautions claim.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current randomized evidence directly supports the specific posterior restriction set when precautions are prescribed and, equally importantly, shows that routine strict precautions should not be generalized as mandatory for every posterior-approach THA patient; NCSBN supports individualized postoperative precaution teaching under Reduction of Risk Potential.
candidate.source_document_title: Do Hip Precautions Matter After Posterior Approach Total Hip Arthroplasty With Capsular Repair? A Randomized Control Trial; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
candidate.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42055222 → Methods: restricted posterior-approach THA group was instructed to avoid hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction past midline, and internal rotation; Results/Conclusions: no significant difference in dislocation risk between restricted and unrestricted groups, so routine strict precautions cannot be presented as universally necessary. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan → Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: evaluate responses to procedures/treatments, use precautions to prevent complications, and provide postoperative teaching based on the prescribed plan of care.
candidate.source_organization: PubMed / Journal of Arthroplasty; National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
candidate.source_version_date: Randomized trial published online 2026-04-27; NCSBN Test Plan effective April 2026
